definition: Vicarious means felt or enjoyed through another person's experience rather than firsthand.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vicarious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vicarious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Too seasick for boats, Ines takes a vicarious delight in her sister's regattas, grilling her for every detail the moment the launch docks.
Interested sits far below vicarious — an interested viewer follows the story but feels none of it as her own.
Invested comes closer but stops short of vicarious — an invested fan cares how it ends, while vicarious excitement makes the finish feel like yours.

Secondhand describes what gets passed along — information, goods, an account relayed through other hands before it reaches you. Vicarious is about feeling: an experience you live through another person, their risk raising your pulse. A secondhand report reaches your ears; a vicarious thrill reaches your nerves.

Borrowed means taken temporarily from someone else, with the understanding it goes back — a coat, an umbrella, a phrase. Vicarious experience is not on loan and is never handed back: you keep the feeling of a race someone else ran. Borrowed marks a loan; vicarious marks a distance.

A vicar originally ministered as the bishop's stand-in, serving a parish in his place — a deputy by definition.
Vicarious means felt or enjoyed through another person's experience rather than firsthand.

The bookshop's 'armchair adventure' shelf sells vicarious experience by the pound: readers who will never leave the county cross the Gobi by camel, round Cape Horn in a gale, and walk into Timbuktu at dusk — all between dinner and bed.
Vicarious experience arrives through another person: their risk, your racing pulse.

The word covers borrowed joys and borrowed sorrows alike — a parent's vicarious nerves at an audition, a fan's vicarious triumph — and it always keeps one honest distance: someone else lived it first.
Vicarious marks experience at one remove: the feeling is real, but the living was someone else's.
It pairs naturally with emotions — vicarious thrill, pride, embarrassment.
Use 'secondhand' for relayed information; keep vicarious for borrowed feeling, the slot English has no plainer word for.

Nobody in the family expected Grandma Ruth to care much about Tomas's exchange year in Chile.
She had never flown anywhere, and she said so often, without regret.
But by October her kitchen wall held a bus map of Valparaiso, and she was living the year at a distance that somehow had no distance in it -- her week rising and falling with his.
When he wrote that he had frozen during a class presentation, she lost a night's sleep; when he finally aced one, she baked as if the grade were hers.
Her daughter called the whole performance vicarious and meant it kindly: Ruth had found a way to travel while never leaving her stove.
